title: Verb and Preposition Patterns: In, Into, With, To and On
summary: Use in, into, with, to and on with common verbs to express convictions and success, entry and movement, division and translation, provision, invitations, preferences, concentration and insistence. Distinguish believe a statement from believe in a principle.
learningObjectives: Distinguish believe somebody or something from believe in an idea, and use specialise in and succeed in + -ing.
Choose into for forced entry, movement towards a collision, dividing a whole and translation into a new language.
Use with after collide, fill and provide or supply, with accurate placement of the recipient and object.
Use to with happen, invite and prefer, and on with concentrate, insist + -ing and spend money.

explanation.heading: Convictions, professional fields and achievement with in
explanation.body: Believe somebody or believe a statement means accept that what is said is true. Believe in a principle, cause or approach means consider it valuable or worthwhile; believe in can also express a belief that something exists. Specialise in introduces a particular area of expertise. Succeed in + -ing explains an achievement after an attempt; do not substitute a bare infinitive after succeed in.
explanation.example: I believe the figures in the report, but I do not believe in making decisions without checking them.

explanation.heading: Entry, movement, division and translation with into
explanation.body: Break into describes entering a building or vehicle without permission, often by force. Crash, drive, run or bump into can mark contact with a physical object; collide with is another possible collision pattern. Divide, cut or split something into parts describes the new groups or pieces. When translating a text from one language into another, from names the source language and into the target language.
explanation.example: The editor divided the handbook into four sections before translating the summary into Spanish.

explanation.heading: Collisions, filling and provision with with
explanation.body: Collide with describes two things striking each other. Fill something with a substance describes putting the substance into it, while be full of describes the resulting state. Provide or supply somebody with something names the recipient before with and the resource afterwards. These patterns help specify relationships clearly rather than simply memorising isolated prepositions.
explanation.example: The organisers provided each visitor with a reusable bottle and filled a large tank with drinking water.

explanation.heading: Events, invitations and preferences with to
explanation.body: Happen to introduces the person or thing affected by an event. Invite somebody to an event or place identifies the destination or occasion of the invitation. Prefer one option to another states a comparison, especially when both alternatives are explicitly named. Do not replace these to patterns with prepositions merely because another construction uses them.
explanation.example: The curator invited the volunteers to a private preview, but most preferred the afternoon session to the evening one.

explanation.heading: Attention, insistence and expenses with on
explanation.body: Concentrate on introduces the task or issue receiving attention. Insist on + noun or -ing expresses a firm demand or refusal to abandon a choice; use the -ing form after this preposition. Spend money on something identifies what the money is used for. These are three distinct meanings that share on, so check the main verb and the following noun or action.
explanation.example: Despite the noisy street, Priya concentrated on her revision while her flatmate insisted on playing music.

comparisons.title: Believing a statement versus supporting an approach

left.label: believe + statement
left.note: The speaker accepts the guide’s words as true.

right.label: believe in + principle
right.example: I believe in learning through practice.
right.note: The speaker considers the method valuable or worthwhile.

comparisons.title: The substance going in versus the resulting state

left.label: fill + container + with
left.example: The cook filled the jar with honey.
left.note: With introduces the substance being added to the jar.

right.label: be full of + contents
right.example: The jar is full of honey.
right.note: Full of describes what the jar contains after filling.

examples.sentence: The analyst specialises in renewable-energy policy.
examples.note: Specialise in marks the area of professional expertise.

examples.sentence: The cyclists succeeded in reaching the shelter before sunset.
examples.note: Succeed in is followed by an -ing form to state a completed achievement.

examples.sentence: A van ran into the garden fence while reversing.
examples.note: Run into marks contact with the object struck.

examples.sentence: The charity supplied the families with winter blankets.
examples.note: Supplied somebody with something introduces the material given.

examples.sentence: We spent most of our travel budget on accommodation.
examples.note: Spend a sum on something names the expenditure category.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I do not believe to her explanation of the accident.
commonMistakes.correct: I do not believe her explanation of the accident.
commonMistakes.why: When the meaning is accepting a statement as true, believe takes its object directly.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The translator translated the leaflet from English in Italian.
commonMistakes.correct: The translator translated the leaflet from English into Italian.
commonMistakes.why: The language of the original follows from, and the target language follows into.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The company provided us of protective clothing.
commonMistakes.correct: The company provided us with protective clothing.
commonMistakes.why: Provide somebody with something uses with before the resource.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The children insisted in visiting the planetarium.
commonMistakes.correct: The children insisted on visiting the planetarium.
commonMistakes.why: Insist on + -ing expresses a firm wish or demand.

studyTips: Say paired believe sentences aloud: believe the news for truth, but believe in a solution for support or conviction.
Draw a simple flow for three into patterns: move into an object, divide into groups, translate from one language into another.
Practise mini-dialogues using invite to, prefer A to B, insist on + -ing, and spend money on an expense.

exercises.prompt: After months of practice, Lena finally succeeded ___ the difficult climbing route.
exercises.feedback: Succeed in + -ing expresses a successful outcome; completing follows in.

exercises.prompt: The workshop divided the participants ___ four small groups.
exercises.feedback: Divide somebody or something into groups identifies the resulting parts.

exercises.prompt: The health centre provides local families ___ free first-aid kits.
exercises.feedback: Provide somebody with something introduces the resource supplied to recipients.

exercises.prompt: I would rather travel by rail; I prefer trains ___ coaches for long journeys.
exercises.feedback: Prefer one thing to another is the target comparison pattern here.

exercises.prompt: The team translated the brochure from Polish ___ Swedish. (Supply the target-language preposition.)
exercises.feedback: Translate from the source language into the target language uses into.

exercises.prompt: The delivery driver accidentally drove ___ a low wall while reversing. (Supply the preposition of contact.)
exercises.feedback: Drive into an obstacle names what the vehicle struck.

exercises.prompt: The manager invited the new employees ___ a welcome lunch. (Supply the event preposition.)
exercises.feedback: Invite somebody to an event introduces the occasion.

exercises.prompt: The students insisted ___ finishing the experiment before going home. (Supply one preposition.)
exercises.feedback: Insist on + -ing expresses a firm wish to continue the task.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The scientist specialises on environmental chemistry.
acceptedAnswers: The scientist specialises in environmental chemistry.
exercises.feedback: Specialise in introduces an area of expertise.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The tank was filled of fresh water before the journey.
acceptedAnswers: The tank was filled with fresh water before the journey.
exercises.feedback: Fill something with a substance uses with before its contents.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: A strange thing happened at my sister yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: A strange thing happened to my sister yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Happen to identifies the person affected by the event.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We spent too much money for parking during the trip.
acceptedAnswers: We spent too much money on parking during the trip.
exercises.feedback: Spend money on a particular expense uses on, not for, in this structure.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use the following exact facts in one present-simple sentence: the journalist / specialise / science reporting. Begin “The journalist” and include in.
acceptedAnswers: The journalist specialises in science reporting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Specialises in introduces the journalist’s professional field.

speakingExercises.prompt: You accept Mira’s account as true. Begin “I believe” and end with “Mira’s account”. Say one complete sentence without a preposition.
speakingExercises.feedback: Believe a report directly expresses accepting it as true, not supporting a principle.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one past-simple sentence using: the committee / divide / the budget / three categories. Begin with “The committee” and use into.
acceptedAnswers: The committee divided the budget into three categories.
speakingExercises.feedback: Divided into describes how one total was separated into parts.

speakingExercises.prompt: A host asks how the charity helped the families. Respond in a past-simple sentence beginning “The charity” using “provided the families with warm blankets”.
acceptedAnswers: The charity provided the families with warm blankets.
speakingExercises.feedback: Provide somebody with something correctly names the recipients and the resource.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the preposition and say the sentence: “They invited us at a workshop on Friday.”
acceptedAnswers: They invited us to a workshop on Friday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Invite somebody to an event uses to.

speakingExercises.prompt: Paraphrase the comparison using prefer: “I like the smaller hall more than the larger hall.” Begin “I prefer”, use “the smaller hall to the larger hall”, and say one sentence.
acceptedAnswers: I prefer the smaller hall to the larger hall.
speakingExercises.feedback: Prefer one alternative to another states the comparison with to.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two present-simple sentences in this order, using full forms: first “Our team / concentrate / accuracy”; second “we / spend / very little money / advertising”. Use on in both.
acceptedAnswers: Our team concentrates on accuracy. We spend very little money on advertising.
speakingExercises.feedback: Concentrates on marks attention, and spend on identifies an expense.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend refuses to leave before the film ends. Describe that insistence in one past-simple sentence. Start “My friend insisted”, use “on staying”, and end “until the film ended”.
acceptedAnswers: My friend insisted on staying until the film ended.
speakingExercises.feedback: Insisted on + -ing expresses a firm preference or demand.

listeningExercises.audioText: I believe the report is accurate, but I do not believe in making decisions without asking questions.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker accepts the report but rejects the principle of deciding without questions.

listeningExercises.audioText: We divided the garden into three sections, then planted fruit trees in the smallest one.
listeningExercises.prompt: Where were the fruit trees planted?
listeningExercises.feedback: Divided into introduces the three sections; the trees went in the smallest.

listeningExercises.audioText: The engineer succeeded in identifying the source of the repeated fault.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words immediately after “engineer”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Succeed in + -ing introduces the action successfully completed.

listeningExercises.audioText: The translation team converted the safety guide from German into Polish for the new staff.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which language did the new version use?
listeningExercises.feedback: Into identifies Polish as the target language; German is the source.

listeningExercises.audioText: A delivery van collided with a parked car outside the warehouse, but nobody was injured.
listeningExercises.feedback: The parked car was stationary; the van collided with it.

listeningExercises.audioText: I preferred the afternoon rehearsal to the morning one, but the director insisted on starting at eight in the morning.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which rehearsal time did the director demand?
listeningExercises.feedback: Despite the speaker’s preference, insisted on starting at eight gives the director’s decision.

listeningExercises.audioText: During the review, the interns concentrated on checking every page for mistakes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word phrase immediately after “interns”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Concentrated on marks what received the interns’ attention.

listeningExercises.audioText: Thieves broke into the rehearsal studio overnight, but no equipment was missing.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase immediately after “Thieves”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Broke into means entered a building without permission.
